statement: By using the substitution $x=\tan\theta$, or otherwise, evaluate $\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}\,dx$.
solution: With $x=\tan\theta$, $dx=\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta$ and $1+x^{2}=\sec^{2}\theta$. The limits become $0$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, and the integral is $\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\tfrac12(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=\bigl[\tfrac{\theta}{2}+\tfrac{\sin2\theta}{4}\bigr]_{0}^{\pi/4}=\tfrac{\pi}{8}+\tfrac14$.
